name: Neuroimaging Techniques
what: This subtopic covers the contemporary methods used to capture images of the brain's structure and activity, including CT, MRI, PET, and fMRI. These techniques are divided into structural methods, which show what the brain looks like, and functional methods, which show what the brain is doing.
why: Neuroimaging has transformed psychology and neuroscience by allowing researchers to study the living brain non-invasively and in real time. Understanding how each technique works and its limitations is necessary for critically evaluating research that uses them.

items.title: I can distinguish between structural and functional neuroimaging techniques
items.what: Structural neuroimaging captures images of the physical structure and composition of the brain, such as the shape, size, and presence of damage. Functional neuroimaging captures images of brain activity, showing which areas are active during specific tasks.
items.why: This distinction is fundamental to understanding what a given piece of neuroimaging evidence can and cannot tell us. Structural scans identify damage; functional scans identify activity patterns.
items.example: A CT scan of a stroke patient shows where brain tissue has died, making it a structural technique. An fMRI scan of a person solving a maths problem shows which brain regions are most active during that task, making it a functional technique.

items.title: I can explain how a CT scan works and identify its benefits and limitations
items.what: Computerised tomography (CT) was developed in the 1970s and works by taking successive 2D x-ray images of the brain in a spiralling motion, then stacking them to produce a 3D image. A contrast dye is ingested beforehand to make brain structures visible.
items.why: CT scans are widely used in clinical settings for detecting haemorrhages, blood clots, cancers, and brain mass loss. Understanding their limitations, including the use of ionising radiation and lower image detail, helps in selecting the right tool for a given purpose.
items.example: A patient brought to the emergency department after a head injury receives a CT scan. The scan reveals a subdural haemorrhage, a bleed between the brain and skull, allowing doctors to act quickly. The image is in black and white and less detailed than an MRI but is obtained rapidly.

items.title: I can explain how an MRI scan works and identify its benefits and limitations
items.what: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses magnetic and radio fields to produce detailed 2D and 3D images of the brain. The magnetic field causes atoms in the brain to move and emit signals that are captured as images. It does not use x-rays.
items.why: MRI produces more detailed and coloured images than CT and does not expose patients to ionising radiation, making it safer for repeated use. However, it cannot be used on patients with metal implants such as pacemakers.
items.example: A researcher studying the structural differences between the brains of people with and without depression uses MRI to measure the volume of the hippocampus in both groups. The detailed images allow precise volumetric comparisons that a CT scan could not provide.

items.title: I can explain how a PET scan works and what it measures
items.what: Positron emission tomography (PET) is a functional neuroimaging technique that involves injecting a radioactive glucose substance into the bloodstream. Active brain regions consume more glucose, and the radioactive tracer emits signals that are detected to produce colour-coded images of brain activity.
items.why: PET scans allow researchers to observe brain activity during specific tasks, linking behaviour and mental processes to particular brain regions in ways that structural imaging cannot.
items.example: A participant is injected with radioactive glucose and placed in a PET scanner, then asked to listen to music. The auditory cortex and related areas appear red on the scan, indicating high activity, while areas not involved in processing music show lower activity in cooler colours such as blue or purple.

items.title: I can explain how fMRI works and why it is now the preferred functional neuroimaging method
items.what: Functional MRI (fMRI) uses the same magnetic and radio field technology as MRI but also tracks changes in blood oxygen levels to measure brain activity. More active regions receive more oxygenated blood, producing colour-coded images of activity without requiring injection of a radioactive substance.
items.why: fMRI is preferred over PET because it produces higher quality images, does not require radioactive tracers, and can still track brain activity in real time during tasks. These advantages make it more suitable for research and repeated use.
items.example: A researcher asks a participant to name pictures of animals while lying in an fMRI scanner. The scan shows high activity in the left frontal lobe around Broca's area during speech production, and in the occipital lobe during visual processing of the images, all without any injection.

items.title: I can compare CT and MRI as structural techniques, and PET and fMRI as functional techniques
items.what: CT uses x-ray imaging and produces black-and-white images, while MRI uses magnetic fields and produces more detailed colour images. PET traces radioactive glucose to measure activity, while fMRI traces oxygen levels using magnetic fields, making it safer and more detailed than PET.
items.why: Understanding the comparative strengths and limitations of each technique allows students to evaluate which method is most appropriate for a given research question or clinical situation.
items.example: A doctor assessing a patient with a suspected brain tumour might use an MRI for its detailed structural images. A researcher studying language processing in real time would choose fMRI over PET to avoid the radioactive tracer while still obtaining high-resolution functional data.
